1.pericope_label: To the angel of the church of Ephesus

schools.summary: Victorinus of Pettau paraphrases the opening of the letter thus: in the first epistle he speaks so, I know that thou sufferest and workest, I see that thou art patient, think not that I am staying long from thee. Of the words about those who say they are Jews and are not, he says that all these things tend to praise, and that no small praise, and that it behoves such men, and such a class, and such elected persons, by all means to be admonished, that they may not be defrauded of such privileges granted to them of God; these few things, he adds, the Lord said that he had against them. On the leaving of the first love and the charge to remember whence thou hast fallen, Victorinus observes that he who falls, falls from a height, and therefore the Lord said whence, because even to the very last works of love must be practised, and this is the principal commandment; and finally, unless this is done, he threatened to remove their candlestick out of its place, that is, to disperse the congregation. Bede says that part of this church he blames and part he praises, according to the character of the name, for Ephesus is said to be interpreted a great fall, as well as my will in it. Of the stars he says, that is, who has you in his right hand and seeks you by his power; and of the walking, who goes about in the midst of you and searches the hearts and the reins of all. On the second verse he says, I know, I see, that is, that thou art diligent in the practice of good works and bearest calmly the insufferable injuries of the wicked, for thou hast diligently examined the words and works of the false Apostles and hast not been willing to give way to them in anything. On the fourth verse he says that in the person of some thou hast forsaken the love which began at first, and if they do not regain it he will deprive them of the promised reward of light; but in others thou hatest the examples of evil men, idolatry that is, and fornication, for these are the deeds of the Nicolaitans, as is shown in what follows. On the call to hear he says the Lord indicates that he writes for all the churches the things which he addresses to them individually, for it was not the Church of the Ephesians alone which, if it did not repent, was to be removed from its place, nor was Satan's seat at Pergamos alone and not rather in every place; in like manner also the other things of the several churches are common to every church. The tree of life, Bede adds, is Christ.

Gill says the church at Ephesus seems to have been founded by the Apostle Paul, who continued there two years, by which means all Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus. It is named first, he says, because it was the largest, most populous and famous, and was nearest to Patmos where John now was, and most known to him, it being the place where he had resided, and it was the place from whence the Gospel came to others and spread itself in lesser Asia; but especially it is first written to because it represented the church in the apostolic age, so that this letter contains the things which are. In its very name, Gill adds, there may be an allusion to the state of this church, either to a word which signifies desire, and which may be expressive of the fervent love of that pure and apostolic church to Jesus Christ at the beginning of it, their eager desire after more knowledge of him and communion with him, after his word and ordinances.

Henry says the first of these epistles is directed to the church of Ephesus, a famous church planted by the apostle Paul and afterwards watered and governed by John, who had his residence very much there. We can hardly think, he says, that Timothy was the angel, or sole pastor and bishop, of this church at this time: that he who was of a very excellent spirit, and naturally cared for the good state of the souls of the people, should become so remiss as to deserve the rebukes given to the ministry of this church. Of the sender he observes that we have here one of the titles given to Christ in his appearance to John in the chapter foregoing, and that the title consists of two parts. First, he that holds the stars in his right hand: the ministers of Christ are under his special care and protection, and it is the honour of God that he knows the number of the stars, calls them by their names, binds the sweet influences of Pleiades and looses the bands of Orion; and it is the honour of the Lord Jesus Christ that the ministers of the gospel, who are greater blessings to the church than the stars are to the world, are in his hand.

Clarke summarises the chapter as containing four epistles, to Ephesus commending their labour and patience and reprehending their having left their first love, to Smyrna commending their piety and promising support in tribulation, to Pergamos commending their steadfastness and reprehending their laxity in ecclesiastical discipline, and to Thyatira commending their charity, faith and patience and reprehending their toleration of Jezebel. He then advertises his readers of four things: first, that he does not perceive any metaphorical or allegorical meaning in the epistles to these Churches; secondly, that he considers the Churches as real, and that their spiritual state is here really and literally pointed out, and that they have no reference to any other state; thirdly, that he considers the angel of the Church as signifying the messenger, the pastor, sent by Christ and his apostles to teach and edify that Church; and fourthly, that he considers what is spoken to this angel as spoken to the whole Church, so that it is not the pastor's particular state that is described, but the states of the people in general under his care. By angel, he says, we are to understand the messenger or person sent by God to preside over this Church, and to him the epistle is directed, not as pointing out his state but the state of the Church under his care; angel of the Church here answers exactly to that officer of the synagogue among the Jews called the messenger of the Church, whose business it was to read, pray and teach in the synagogue. The Church at Ephesus is first addressed as being the place where John chiefly resided, the city itself being the metropolis of that part of Asia; and the angel or bishop at this time was most probably Timothy, who presided over that Church before St John took up his residence there, and who is supposed to have continued in that office till near the end of the century and to have been martyred a short time before St John's return from Patmos. He that holdeth the seven stars, Clarke says, particularly preserves, guides and upholds not only the ministers of those seven Churches but all the genuine ministers of his Gospel in all ages and places; and he that walketh in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks is the supreme Bishop and Head, not only of those Churches, but of all the Churches or congregations of his people throughout the world. Wesley says Christ dictated to John every word. These things saith he who holdeth the seven stars in his right hand: such is his mighty power, such his favour to them and care over them, that they may indeed shine as stars, both by purity of doctrine and holiness of life. Who walketh, according to his promise, I am with you always, even to the end of the world; in the midst of the golden candlesticks, beholding all their works and thoughts, and ready to remove the candlestick out of its place if any, being warned, will not repent. Perhaps here is likewise an allusion, Wesley adds, to the office of the priests in dressing the lamps, which was to keep them always burning before the Lord.

Barnes says this chapter comprises four of the seven epistles addressed to the seven churches, those to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos and Thyatira, and offers some general remarks on their structure. They all begin with a reference to some of the attributes of the Saviour, in general some attribute that had been noted in the first chapter; and while they are all adapted to make a deep impression on the mind, perhaps each one was selected in such a way as to have a special propriety in reference to each particular church. Thus in the address to Ephesus the allusion is to the fact that he who speaks to them holds the seven stars in his right hand and walks in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks; in the epistle to Smyrna it is he who is the first and the last, who was dead and is alive; in the epistle to Pergamos it is he which hath the sharp sword with the two edges; and in the epistle to Thyatira it is the Son of God, who hath his eyes like a flame of fire. Ellicott says that, adopting the view that the angel represents the chief pastor or bishop of the Church, it would be interesting to know who was its presiding minister at this time, but that this must be determined by another question, namely the date of the Apocalypse. Accepting the earlier date, that is, the reign of Nero, or with Gebhardt of Galba, the angel is no other than Timothy, and some striking coincidences favour this view: labour, work and endurance are what St Paul acknowledges in Timothy and exhorts him to cultivate more and more; against false teachers he warns him; and further, there is a latent tone of anxiety in the Epistles to Timothy, the nature with which he had to do being emotional even to tears, ascetic and devout, but with a tendency to lack of energy and sustained enthusiasm, so that, as Professor Plumptre puts it, he urges him to stand up, to rekindle the grace of God, just as here there is a hint of a first love left. Of the city Ellicott says Ephesus was the chief city of Ionia and at this time the most important city in Asia, possessing advantages commercial, geographical and ecclesiastical. Robertson says Ephesus lay near the sea on the river Cayster, the foremost city of Asia Minor, the temple-keeper of Artemis and her wonderful temple, the home of the magic arts and of the mystery-cults, the place of Paul's three years' stay, where Aquila and Priscilla and Apollos laboured, where Timothy wrought, and where the Apostle John preached in his old age; surely it was a place of great privilege and of great preaching. It was about sixty miles from Patmos, and the messenger would reach Ephesus first; it was a free city and a seat of proconsular government, the end of the great road from the Euphrates. The port was a place of shifting sands, due to the silting up of the mouth of the Cayster, and Ramsay calls it the City of Change. The demonstrative rendered these things occurs seven times here, once with the message to each church, and only once elsewhere in the New Testament. He that holdeth is the present active articular participle of a stronger word than the having of the first chapter, to which it refers, and he that walketh is an allusion to the same vision, these two epithets being drawn from it.

debates: Who the angel of Ephesus was: Clarke thinks it most probably Timothy, who presided before John came to reside there, and Ellicott agrees on the earlier dating of the book, citing Plumptre on the coincidences of labour, warnings against false teachers and a latent tone of anxiety; Henry refuses the identification outright, saying one of so excellent a spirit could hardly have become remiss enough to deserve these rebukes

Whether the letters carry a further meaning: Clarke advertises his readers that he perceives no metaphorical or allegorical meaning in them and considers the churches as real, their spiritual state literally pointed out, where Gill holds Ephesus is written to first because it represented the church in the apostolic age and finds an allusion in the very name to a word signifying desire

What the angel means: Clarke takes it as the pastor, answering to the synagogue officer whose business was to read, pray and teach, and insists that what is said to him describes not his own state but the people's under his care; Ellicott takes it as the chief pastor or bishop

How far the letters reach: Bede holds that what is addressed to each church is written for all, since Satan's seat was not at Pergamos alone but in every place, and Clarke likewise extends the two titles to all the ministers and congregations of Christ's people throughout the world
outliers: Bede's reading of the name Ephesus as both a great fall and my will in it
Clarke's identification of the angel with the sheliach tsibbur, the synagogue's messenger who read, prayed and taught
Ellicott's report from Plumptre that Timothy's nature was emotional even to tears, ascetic and devout, yet lacking sustained enthusiasm
Henry's use of Pleiades and Orion, that he who binds their influences knows the number and names of the stars
Ramsay's name for Ephesus, quoted by Robertson, the City of Change, from the silting of the Cayster
Victorinus's remark that he who falls, falls from a height, which is why the Lord said whence
Wesley's suspicion of an allusion to the priests dressing the lamps, whose work was to keep them always burning

2.pericope_label: I know thy works: labour, patience, and a love left

schools.summary: Gill says the works known are the good works both of ministers and churches, no evil works being mentioned, nor anything complained of in this church but an abatement of the fervour of her first love. Christ, as the omniscient God, knows all the works of his people, and the springs and principles and ends and views of them, whether they are done in obedience to him, spring from love to him, are performed in his strength and by his grace and directed to his glory; such he takes notice of, approves of and is well pleased with, not as the ground of his delight in their persons but as the fruits of his own grace. During the apostolic age, Gill adds, churches and ministers were very diligent in working, yea, they were laborious. Of the bearing he says the object is not evil men nor false apostles but burdens, as the Ethiopic version reads and as the word signifies, meaning afflictions, reproaches and persecutions, which pressed sore and lay heavy on these ministers and churches; yet they bore them with constancy and cheerfulness and were not moved by them, while the Arabic version reads instead, and thou hast borne me, that is, my name and Gospel, among the Gentiles. On the complaint he notes that the Jews represent God saying concerning their fathers, I have something against them; Christ has nothing against his people, his faithful ministers and true churches, in a judicial way or to their condemnation, for there is no condemnation to them that are in him, but he has often many things to complain of in them, and to rebuke and chastise them for, in a way of providence.

Clarke says the eyes of the Lord are throughout the earth, beholding the evil and the good, and being omnipresent, all things are continually open and naked before him. It is worthy of remark, he says, that whatsoever is praiseworthy in any of these Churches is first mentioned, thereby intimating that God is more intent on finding out the good than the evil in any person or Church, and that those who wish to reform such as have fallen, or are not making sufficient advances in the Divine life, should take occasion from the good which yet remains to encourage them to set out afresh for the kingdom of heaven; the fallen or backsliding who have any tenderness of conscience left are easily discouraged. Of the third verse he says it repeats the same things mentioned in the preceding verse, but in an inverted order, the particular reason of which does not appear; perhaps it was intended to show more forcibly to this Church that there was no good which they had done, nor evil which they had suffered, that was forgotten before God. And hast not fainted, he adds, shows they must have had a considerable portion of this love remaining, else they could not have thus acted. The clause about the complaint should be read, according to the Greek, thus: but I have against thee that thou hast left thy first love; they did not retain that strong and ardent affection for God and sacred things which they had when first brought to the knowledge of the truth and justified by faith in Christ. Wesley says Jesus knows all the good and all the evil which his servants and his enemies suffer and do, and calls it a weighty word, I know: how dreadful will it one day sound to the wicked, how sweet to the righteous. The churches and their angels must have been astonished to find their several states so exactly described, even in the absence of the apostle, and could not but acknowledge the all-seeing eye of Christ and of his Spirit; and with regard to us, to every one of us also he saith, I know thy works. Happy is he, Wesley adds, that conceives less good of himself than Christ knows concerning him. After the general term, three particulars are named and then more largely described in an inverted order. Of the fault he says it is the love for which all that church was so eminent when St Paul wrote his epistle to them: he need not have left this, and might have retained it entire to the end, and he did retain it in part, or there could not have remained so much of what was commendable in him; but he had not kept, as he might have done, the first tender love in its vigour and warmth. Reader, Wesley asks, hast thou?

Barnes says the formula I know thy works is common to all the epistles to the seven churches, designed to impress upon them deeply the conviction that he was intimately acquainted with all that they did, good and bad, and that he was therefore abundantly qualified to dispense rewards or administer punishments according to truth and justice. Since many of the things referred to in these epistles pertain to the heart, the feelings, the state of the mind, it is implied that he who speaks here has an intimate acquaintance with the heart of man, a prerogative always attributed to the Saviour; but no one can do this who is not Divine. Of the bearing he says they had borne up under trials and borne with the evils with which they were assailed, not giving way to murmuring or complaints in trial, nor abandoning the principles of truth and yielding to the prevalence of error; and that where the second verse referred rather to the trouble experienced on account of the pretensions of false apostles, here the expression is more general, denoting a patient spirit in regard to trials at large. Of the complaint he says that, notwithstanding this general commendation, there are things which cannot be approved: they had remitted or let down their early love, so that it was less glowing and ardent than at first. The love referred to is evidently love to the Saviour, and the idea is that as a church they had less of this than formerly characterised them; in this respect they were in a state of declension, and though they still maintained the doctrines of his religion and opposed the advocates of error, they showed less ardour of affection towards him directly than they had formerly done. Ellicott says the phrase I know thy works is probably common to all the epistles, and expresses the way in which all actions are naked and open before those flame-like eyes of him with whom we have to do: the veneer of a formal faith might impose on the world, but it would not escape his scrutiny; he knows too, and lovingly accepts, the unmarked and unrequited acts of true love, and appreciates, amid all its failures, genuine loyalty to him. The labour and patience are the same things which St Paul had pressed on Timothy. Of the third verse Ellicott says it needs some change to bring it into harmony with the best manuscripts, and should stand, and hast patience, and didst bear for my name's sake, and didst not weary; in this last word there is a recurrence to the word translated labour or toil in the second verse, since they had toiled on to very weariness without wearying of their toil, just as they could not bear the evil and yet had borne reproaches for Christ's sake. He quotes Dr Vaughan: there is toil, and patience, and abhorrence of evil, and discernment, and again patience, and endurance, and unwearied exertion; what can be wanting here? Of the fault he says the rendering should be, I have against thee that thou didst let go, and that this is no trifle which is blamed, as the word somewhat, which is not to be found in the original, might be taken to imply; for the decay of love is the decay of that without which all other graces are as nothing, since, as Norman Macleod put it, all religion is summed up in one word, Love: God asks this, we cannot give more, he cannot take less. Great as the fault is, Ellicott adds, it is the fault which Love alone would have detected, and he asks whether any one can more touchingly rebuke than by commencing, thou no longer lovest me enough, calling it the regretful cry of the heavenly Bridegroom recalling the early days. Robertson says the verb for knowing emphasises, in Swete's words, the absolute clearness of mental vision which photographs all the facts of life as they pass, and that where the other verb stands the universal knowledge passes into the field of special observation. Works means the whole life and conduct; toil and patience are given in explanation of works, all three words occurring together in First Thessalonians, and there is a sharp distinction between activities and toils attended with weariness, so that the endurance is endurance in hard toil. Thou hast is continued possession of patience; didst bear is a first aorist referring back to the crisis of the second verse; and hast not grown weary is a perfect active of an old verb, a play on the word for toil, with the late ending shared by two other verbs in these verses. Robertson quotes Moffatt, that they were tired in loyalty, not of it, and that the Ephesian church can bear anything except the presence of impostors in her membership. Of the complaint he says the clause is the object of the verb have, that the aorist marks a definite and sad departure, and that this early love, the proof of the new life in Christ, had cooled off in spite of their doctrinal purity: they had remained orthodox but had become unloving, partly because of the controversies with the Nicolaitans.

debates: How much the word somewhat concedes: Ellicott insists it is not in the original and that nothing trifling is blamed, since the decay of love is the decay of that without which all other graces are nothing, where the received rendering invites the reader to treat the charge as slight

Whether any of the first love remained: Clarke argues from the words hast not fainted that a considerable portion must have remained, else they could not have acted as they did, and Wesley agrees that it was retained in part though not in its first vigour and warmth, while Barnes describes the church simply as in a state of declension

What caused the cooling: Robertson traces it to the controversies with the Nicolaitans, so that they remained orthodox and became unloving, where Barnes leaves it as a general decline of ardour and Gill treats it as an abatement of fervour rather than a fault of doctrine

What the third verse should read: Ellicott holds the best manuscripts give, and hast patience, and didst bear for my name's sake, and didst not weary, recovering a play on the word for toil, where Clarke keeps the received order and explains the inversion as a sign that no good done and no evil suffered was forgotten
outliers: Clarke's rule that the praiseworthy is always named first, since God is more intent on finding the good than the evil
Ellicott's citation of Norman Macleod, that God asks love, we cannot give more, and he cannot take less
Ellicott's question, whether anyone can rebuke more touchingly than by beginning, thou no longer lovest me enough
Moffatt's phrase, quoted by Robertson, that they were tired in loyalty and not of it
Swete's image, quoted by Robertson, of a mental vision which photographs all the facts of life as they pass
Vaughan's question, quoted by Ellicott, what can be wanting here?
Wesley's turn upon the reader, hast thou kept the first tender love in its vigour and warmth?

5.pericope_label: Remember, repent, and the promise of the tree of life

schools.summary: Gill says believers cannot totally and finally fall away from the grace which they have received, but they may fall into sin, and from a degree of grace and the exercise of it, as these first and pure churches did, from some degree of their love to God and Christ and one another; and therefore they are called upon to remember, mind and observe from what degree of it they were fallen, in order to bring them under a conviction and acknowledgment of their evil and a sense of their present state, and to quicken their desires after a restoration to their former one. Of the Nicolaitans he says that though these Christians had left their first love, yet they bore a hatred to the filthy and impure practices of some men who were called Nicolaitans, who committed fornication, adultery and all uncleanness, had their wives in common, and also ate things offered to idols; who were so called, as some think, from Nicolas of Antioch, one of the seven deacons. Though as to Nicolas himself, Gill adds, it is said that he lived with his own lawful married wife and no other, that his daughters continued virgins all their days and his son incorrupt, and that these men so called only shrouded themselves under his name. Of the ear he says it means such as have new ears given them, as all have who are made new creatures, whose ears are circumcised and opened by the Spirit of God, who hear with understanding, affection and faith, who try what they hear and approve, embrace and retain that which is good.

Clarke says the charge to remember means, consider the state of grace in which you once stood, the happiness, love and joy which you felt when ye received remission of sins, the zeal ye had for God's glory and the salvation of mankind, your willing obedient spirit, your cheerful self-denial, your fervour in private prayer, your detachment from the world and your heavenly-mindedness: remember, consider, all these. Whence thou art fallen means fallen from all those blessed dispositions and gracious feelings already mentioned; or, remember what a loss you have sustained, for so the Greek verb is frequently used by the best Greek writers. Repent means, be deeply humbled before God for having so carelessly guarded the Divine treasure. The Nicolaitans he takes to have been, as is commonly supposed, a sect of the Gnostics, who taught the most impure doctrines and followed the most impure practices, and who are also supposed to have derived their origin from Nicolas, one of the seven deacons; they taught the community of wives, that adultery and fornication were things indifferent, that eating meats offered to idols was quite lawful, and mixed several pagan rites with the Christian ceremonies, Augustine, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian having spoken largely concerning them. He that hath an ear means, let every intelligent person and every Christian man attend carefully to what the Holy Spirit in this and the following epistles says to the Churches; and to him that overcometh means to him who continues steadfast in the faith and uncorrupt in his life, who faithfully confesses Jesus and neither imbibes the doctrines nor is led away by the error of the wicked. As he who conquered his enemies had generally not only great honour but also a reward, Clarke says, so here a great reward is promised to the conqueror, and there may be an allusion to the Grecian games. Wesley says it is not possible for any to recover the first love but by taking three steps: remember, repent, and do the first works. Remember from whence thou art fallen, that is, from what degree of faith, love and holiness, though perhaps insensibly; and repent, which in the very lowest sense implies a deep and lively conviction of thy fall. Of the seven angels, he observes, two, at Ephesus and at Pergamos, were in a mixed state; two, at Sardis and at Laodicea, were greatly corrupted, and all these are exhorted to repent, as are the followers of Jezebel at Thyatira; two, at Smyrna and Philadelphia, were in a flourishing state and are therefore only exhorted to steadfastness. Of the Nicolaitans Wesley says divine grace seeks whatever may help him that is fallen to recover his standing, and that they were probably so called from Nicolas, one of the seven deacons, their doctrines and lives being equally corrupt: they allowed the most abominable lewdness and adulteries, as well as sacrificing to idols, all which they placed among things indifferent and pleaded for as branches of Christian liberty. He that hath an ear, Wesley says, means every man, whoever can hear at all, ought carefully to hear this; and to him that overcometh means to every one that goeth on from faith and by faith to full victory over the world, the flesh and the devil. In these seven letters twelve promises are contained, which are an extract of all the promises of God: some of them are not expressly mentioned again in this book, as the hidden manna, the inscription of the name of the new Jerusalem, the sitting upon the throne, while some resemble what is afterwards mentioned.

Barnes says the duty enjoined is that, when religion has declined in our hearts or in the church, we should call to distinct recollection the former state, the ardour, the zeal, the warmth of love which once characterised us; the reason is that such a recalling of the former state will be likely to produce a happy influence on the heart, since nothing is better adapted to affect a backsliding Christian, or a backsliding church, than to call to distinct recollection the happier days of piety, the joy then experienced and the good then done. Of the Nicolaitans he says the word occurs only here and in a later verse of this chapter, and that from the reference in the latter place it is clear the doctrines they held prevailed at Pergamos as well as at Ephesus; but from neither place can anything now be inferred in regard to the nature of their doctrines or their practices, unless it be supposed that they held the same doctrine that was taught by Balaam. From the two passages compared with each other it would seem that they were alike corrupt in doctrine and in practice. Of the closing summons he says the expression occurs at the close of each of the epistles addressed to the seven churches, and is substantially a mode of address often employed by the Saviour in his personal ministry and quite characteristic of him, designed to arrest the attention and to denote that what was said was of special importance; what the Spirit saith is evidently what the Holy Spirit says, for he is regarded in the Scriptures as the Source of inspiration and as appointed to disclose truth to man, and the Spirit may be regarded either as speaking through the Saviour or as imparting the truth directly. Ellicott says it is argued that we have here evidence that the later, or Domitian, date of the Apocalypse is the true one, since it describes a fall in spiritual life which might have occurred in thirty years but would hardly have taken place in the few years, ten at the utmost, which elapsed between the visit of St Paul and the reign of Nero. But greater changes than a decay of this kind, he answers, have passed over communities in equally short periods: we have seen nations pass from imperialism to republicanism, from the fever-heat of radicalism to the lethargy of conservatism, in shorter space. The Nicolaitans, Ellicott says, were the Antinomians of the Asiatic Church: the life and conduct were little thought of, and the faith professed was everything. Some have thought that they were a sect who derived their name, under some colourable pretext, from Nicolas the Proselyte; others hold that the name is purely symbolical, signifying destroyer of the people, and that it is no more than the Greek form of Balaam. The existence of a sect called Nicolaitanes in the second century is attested by Irenaeus, Tertullian and Clement of Alexandria. Of the summons to hear he says these words, an echo from the Gospels, recur in all the seven epistles, but that in the first three they are placed before the promise and in the remaining four they follow it. The heart which is hardened is the precursor of the ear that is deaf, and the spiritual truth needs a spiritual organ for its discernment: these are truths, then, only heard, as Coleridge has it, when the soul seeks to hear, when all is hushed, and the heart listens. Robertson says remember is a present active imperative meaning continue mindful, and thou art fallen a perfect indicative marking a state of completion, so that, down in the valley, one is to look up to the cliff where pure love is and whence he has fallen down; and repent is a first aorist imperative, an urgent appeal for instant change of attitude and conduct before it is too late, while do is likewise aorist, meaning do at once, the first works including the first love which has now grown cold. Of the hatred he says the clause is an accusative object in apposition, and that Trench tells of the words used in ancient Greek for hatred of evil and for a hater of evil, neither of which occurs in the New Testament, but which accurately describe the angel of the church in Ephesus. Irenaeus and Hippolytus, he adds, take the sect to be followers of Nicolaus of Antioch, one of the seven deacons, a Jewish proselyte who is said to have apostatised; there was such a sect in the second century, but whether descended from Nicolaus of Antioch is not certain. He that hath an ear is an individualising note calling on each of the hearers to listen, and a reminiscence of the words of Jesus in the Synoptics, but not in John's Gospel; the Spirit is the Holy Spirit, so that both Christ and the Holy Spirit deliver this message, and as Swete says, the Spirit of Christ in the prophet is the interpreter of Christ's voice. To him that overcometh is the dative of a present active articular participle, marking continuous victory, of a verb common in the Johannine writings.

debates: Whether the decay dates the book: Ellicott reports the argument that so great a fall proves the later Domitian date, since ten years at most separated Paul's visit from Nero's reign, and answers that greater changes have passed over communities in shorter periods, nations moving from imperialism to republicanism and from the fever-heat of radicalism to the lethargy of conservatism

Who the Nicolaitans were: Clarke and Wesley take them as followers of Nicolas the deacon, Gill reports the same derivation but defends Nicolas himself as having lived with one lawful wife and left virgin daughters and an incorrupt son, Ellicott offers the alternative that the name is symbolical, destroyer of the people and the Greek of Balaam, and Robertson doubts any descent from the deacon can be established

How much can be known of their teaching: Barnes holds that nothing can now be inferred from these two passages about their doctrines or practices unless they held what Balaam taught, where Clarke lists community of wives, indifference to fornication, meats offered to idols and pagan rites mixed with Christian ceremonies

How far the falling goes: Gill insists that believers cannot totally and finally fall from grace, only from a degree of it and its exercise, where Wesley makes recovery depend on three steps that must actually be taken, and Robertson reads the perfect tense as a settled state to be looked up out of
outliers: Clarke's inventory of what is to be remembered, down to fervour in private prayer and detachment from the world
Coleridge's lines, quoted by Ellicott, that such truths are heard when all is hushed and the heart listens
Gill's defence of Nicolas of Antioch, whose daughters continued virgins and whose son was incorrupt
