8.pericope_label: To Smyrna: poverty, ten days of tribulation, the crown of life

schools.summary: Gill says there was without doubt a church of Christ at Smyrna, though by whom it was founded is not certain, very likely by the Apostle Paul, who was in those parts and by whose means all Asia heard the Gospel of Christ. Some think the present angel or pastor of this church was Polycarp, the disciple of John; Irenaeus, who knew him, says he was appointed bishop of Smyrna by the apostles, and here he suffered martyrdom and was buried, the large amphitheatre in which he was put to death being still to be seen and his sepulchre yet preserved in this place, besides a very famous epistle sent by this church concerning his sufferings. Of the tribulation Gill says God's people undergo sufferings of various sorts, as the Christians of those times did, scourgings, imprisonment, confiscation of goods and death itself in various shapes; these are certain, they shall suffer them, they are all known beforehand to Christ, and he sometimes gives his people previous notice of them, nor should they indulge a slavish fear about them. It is reported of Polycarp, bishop of this church at Smyrna, in a letter written by the church itself, that three days before he suffered he dreamed his pillow, on which he laid his head, was on fire, upon which, awaking, he said to those that were by him that he should be burnt alive. Of the works known Gill says only that they are good works, as before.

Henry says the second epistle is directed to the angel of the church in Smyrna, a place well known at this day by our merchants, a city of great trade and wealth, perhaps the only city of all the seven that is still known by the same name, now however no longer distinguished for its Christian church, being overrun by Mahomedism. The subscription, he says, contains another of the glorious titles of our Lord Jesus, the first and the last, he that was dead and is alive, taken out of the first chapter.

Clarke says the angel here was probably the famous Polycarp, and that of the title, these things saith the first and the last, we are to understand him who is eternal, from whom all things come and to whom all things must return, who was dead for the redemption of the world and is alive to die no more for ever, his glorified humanity being enthroned at the Father's right hand. Of the works he says, as he had spoken to the preceding Church so he speaks to this: I know all that ye have done and all that ye have suffered. The tribulation must mean persecution, either from the Jews, the heathens, or from the heretics, who because of their flesh-pampering doctrines might have had many partisans at Smyrna; and the poverty means they were stripped probably of all their temporal possessions because of their attachment to the Gospel, though they were rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom of Christ. There were persons there, he says, who professed Judaism and had a synagogue in the place and professed to worship the true God, but they were no true Jews. The charge not to fear may be addressed particularly to Polycarp, if he was at that time the bishop of this Church: he had much to suffer and was at last burnt alive at Smyrna about the year one hundred and sixty-six. We have a very ancient account of his martyrdom, Clarke says, which has been translated by Cave and is worthy of the reader's perusal; that account states that the Jews were particularly active in this martyrdom and brought the faggots by which he was consumed, and such persons must indeed have been of the synagogue of Satan. As the days in this book are what is commonly called prophetic days, each answering to a year, the ten days of tribulation may mean ten years. Of the promise he says the conqueror is he who has stood firm in every trial and vanquished all his adversaries, and that not to be hurt of the second death means an eternal separation from God and the glory of his power, what we commonly mean by final perdition; this is another rabbinical mode of speech in very frequent use, and by it they understand the punishment of hell in a future life. Wesley says the description of him who was dead and is alive tends directly to confirm the angel against the fear of death, and that with the very comfort wherewith St John himself was comforted shall the angel of this church be comforted. Of the affliction and poverty he says it is a poor prerogative in the eyes of the world, since the angel at Philadelphia likewise had in their sight but a little strength, and yet these two were the most honourable of all in the eyes of the Lord; but thou art rich, he says, in faith and love, of more value than all the kingdoms of the earth. Those who say they are Jews claim to be God's own people and are not, being not Jews inwardly nor circumcised in heart, but a synagogue of Satan, who, like them, was a liar and a murderer from the beginning. The first and last words of the tenth verse, Wesley observes, are particularly directed to the minister, whence we may gather that his suffering and the affliction of the church were at the same time and of the same continuance; the word behold intimates the nearness of the affliction, and perhaps the ten days began on the very day that the Revelation was read at Smyrna, or at least very soon after. The devil is he who sets all persecutors to work, and these more particularly; and the second death is the lake of fire, the portion of the fearful who do not overcome.

Barnes says the idea in the title is that he is a living Saviour, and that there was a propriety in referring to that fact here from the nature of the promise about to be made, that he who overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death: as he had himself triumphed over death in all its forms and was now alive for ever, it was appropriate that he should promise his true friends the same protection. Of the works he says the uniform method of introducing these epistles implies a most intimate acquaintance with all that pertained to the church; tribulation is of general signification and probably includes all that they suffered in any form, whether from persecution, poverty, or the blasphemy of opposers. It would seem that this church at that time was eminently poor, for this is not specified in regard to any one of the others, and no reason is suggested why they were particularly poor, though it was not an uncommon characteristic of early Christians. Of the charge not to fear he says the Saviour did not promise them exemption from suffering: he saw that they were about to suffer and specifies the manner in which their affliction would occur, but entreats and commands them not to be afraid, since they were to look to the crown of life and to be comforted with the assurance that if they were faithful unto death that would be theirs. The particular promise at the close is made to him that should overcome, that is, gain the victory in the persecutions which were to come upon them, showing the sustaining power of religion in times of persecution, not yielding his principles when opposed and persecuted, and triumphing when so many efforts were made to induce him to apostatise; not to be hurt of the second death means he will have nothing to fear in the future world, the punishment of hell being often called death, not in the sense that the soul will cease to exist. Ellicott describes Smyrna as the modern Ismir, now possessing a population of about a hundred and fifty thousand, its mercantile prosperity measurable by its trade, the export trade in one recent year amounting to more than a million and three-quarter pounds, about half of this being with England, and the imports in the same year somewhat less. It has always been considered one of the most beautiful cities in Asia; it was situated in the ancient province of Ionia, a little north of Ephesus, next it, as Archbishop Trench says, in natural order and also in spiritual; its position was favourable for commerce, and in olden times as now it commanded the trade of the Levant, besides being the natural outlet for the produce of the Hermus valley, the neighbourhood being peculiarly fertile. Of the phrase I know thy works he says some would omit the word works, but it is admitted to be genuine in five out of the seven epistles, and it seems natural to conclude that it was intended to be common to all, reminding the Christian communities that whatever their state it was known to him whose eyes were as a flame of fire; and he quotes Bengel, that we go from one hour to another, from one day and year to another, and what is once fairly past in our doing and omitting and suffering is scarcely regarded by us any more, being like water that has flowed away, but into the omniscience of Christ all things are taken up. Though Christ proclaimed his yoke to be easy, Ellicott says, he also said that his followers must expect tribulation, and he never conceals the difficulties or dangers of his service. The name devil is given to Satan in the Greek Old Testament, regarding him as the accuser; and of the trial he says that on the part of the adversary the intention was that they might be tempted from their allegiance to Christ, while the real effect would be that they who endured would come forth tested. Of the promise he says the words used are precise and give certainty to it, and that the phrase second death is a new one in Bible language, said to have been familiar to the Jews through its use in the Chaldee Paraphrase; it clearly points to a death which is other than that of the body and stands in contrast with the crown of life, and the expressions of the twentieth and twenty-first chapters exclude the idea that a cessation of conscious existence is intended, since the life of the spirit is the knowledge of God and the death of the spirit is the decay or paralysis of the powers by which such knowledge was possible. Robertson says Smyrna lay north of Ephesus on a gulf of the Aegean, one of the great cities of the province, a seat of emperor-worship with a temple to Tiberius, with many Jews hostile to Christianity who later join in the martyrdom of Polycarp, a poor church rich in grace which receives only praise from Christ; Ramsay terms Smyrna the City of Life, and Christianity has held on here better than in any city of Asia. The title repeats the language of the first chapter, and the phrase rendered which was dead is rather, who became dead. The tribulation and the poverty have separate articles of the same gender, emphasising each item; the tribulation was probably persecution, which helped to intensify the poverty of the Christians, in contrast with the wealthy church in Laodicea, the parenthesis but thou art rich showing the spiritual riches of this church against the spiritual poverty of that, this a rich poor church and that a poor rich church, rich in grace toward God and in good deeds; and perhaps Jews and pagans had pillaged their property, poor as they already were. Fear not is as in the first chapter, worse things being about to come than poverty and blasphemy, perhaps prison and death, for the devil is going to cast; the purpose clause gives the trial, and John himself is in exile, Peter and John having often been in prison together, while James the brother of John, Paul and Peter had all suffered martyrdom. Shall not be hurt is a strong double negative with an old verb meaning to act unjustly, here to do harm or wrong to one; of the second death is explained later as the lake of fire, the idea being present in Daniel and John and current in Jewish circles as in the Jerusalem Targum on Deuteronomy and in Philo. It is not annihilation, Robertson says: the Christians put to death in the persecution will at least escape this second death.

debates: How long the ten days are: Clarke takes the days of this book as prophetic days each answering to a year, so that ten years of tribulation are meant, where Wesley reads them literally and suspects they may have begun on the very day the Revelation was read at Smyrna

Who the angel of Smyrna was: Clarke says probably the famous Polycarp and Gill reports the same on the authority of Irenaeus, who knew him and says the apostles appointed him bishop there, while Barnes and Ellicott name no one

What the second death is: Ellicott calls the phrase new in Bible language and argues from the later chapters that no cessation of conscious existence is meant, defining it as the decay of the powers by which the knowledge of God was possible; Robertson says flatly that it is not annihilation; Clarke calls it a rabbinical mode of speech for the punishment of hell; Barnes says death is used here without implying the soul will cease to exist

Why this church alone is called poor: Barnes notes the fact is specified of no other and that no reason is suggested, Clarke supposes them stripped of their possessions for their attachment to the Gospel, Robertson guesses at pillage by Jews and pagans, and Wesley treats the poverty itself as the mark of honour
outliers: Bengel's image, quoted by Ellicott, that what is past in our doing and suffering is like water that has flowed away, yet into the omniscience of Christ all things are taken up
Gill's report of Polycarp's dream of his burning pillow three days before his death
Ramsay's name for Smyrna, quoted by Robertson, the City of Life
Robertson's antithesis, that this is a rich poor church and Laodicea a poor rich one
The ancient account of Polycarp's martyrdom, cited by Clarke from Cave, that the Jews themselves brought the faggots
Trench's remark, quoted by Ellicott, that Smyrna follows Ephesus in natural order and also in spiritual
Wesley's observation that Smyrna and Philadelphia, least esteemed by the world, were most honourable in the eyes of the Lord

12.pericope_label: To Pergamos: Satan’s throne, Antipas, and the doctrine of Balaam

schools.summary: Gill says there was a church of Christ in Pergamos, but when it began and how long it lasted is not certain. Antipas, who is mentioned, is thought by some to have been the pastor of it, though according to the Apostolical Constitutions Caius was the first bishop; and it appears that in the second century there were several in this place who suffered martyrdom for Christ, as Carpus, Papulus, and a woman whose name was Agathonice, while Attalus the martyr, who suffered in the same century, was also a native of this place. In the fifth century there was a bishop of Pergamos in the council at Ephesus. Of the works he says they are both good and bad, and that in that pure part of this church which opposed the growing corruptions of antichrist they were for the most part good. Of the complaint he says it concerns the members of this church before their open separation from the apostasy, who still continued in the communion of the corrupt church of Rome, though they remonstrated against the errors and evil practices that crept in, and so were a stumbling block and a snare to others to join in their idolatry and superstition.

Henry says that whether Pergamos was a city raised up out of the ruins of old Troy, a Troy nouveau, as our London was once called, or some other city of the same name, is neither certain nor material; it was a place where Christ had called and constituted a gospel church, by the preaching of the gospel and the grace of his Spirit making the word effectual. The message is sent by the same Jesus who here describes himself as one that hath the sharp sword with two edges, out of whose mouth, as the first chapter has it, went a sharp two-edged sword.

Clarke says the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, cuts every way: it convinces of sin, righteousness and judgment, pierces between the joints and the marrow, divides between the soul and spirit, dissects the whole mind and exhibits a regular anatomy of the soul; it not only reproves and exposes sin, but it slays the ungodly, pointing out and determining the punishment they shall endure. Jesus has the sword with the two edges, Clarke says, because he is the Saviour of sinners and the Judge of quick and dead. Where Satan's seat is means where Satan has his throne, where he reigns as king and is universally obeyed; and it was a maxim among the Jews that where the law of God was not studied, there Satan dwelt, but that he was obliged to leave the place where a synagogue or academy was established. Notwithstanding that the profession of Christianity exposed this Church to the bitterest persecution, they held fast the name of Christian which they had received from Jesus Christ and did not deny his faith, for when brought to the trial they openly professed themselves disciples and followers of their Lord and Master. Of the complaint Clarke says their good deeds are first carefully sought out and commended, and what was wrong in them is touched with a gentle but effectual hand; the followers of Balaam, the Nicolaitans and the Gnostics were probably all the same kind of persons. It appears that there were some then in the Church at Pergamos who held eating things offered to idols in honour of those idols, and fornication, to be indifferent things, and who associated with idolaters in the heathen temples and partook with them in their religious festivals. Wesley says the sword is that with which Christ will cut off the impenitent. Where the throne of Satan is means that Pergamos was above measure given to idolatry, so Satan had his throne and full residence there; and thou holdest fast my name means openly and resolutely confessing me before men. Antipas he takes to have been martyred under Domitian, and says, happy is he to whom Jesus, the faithful and true witness, giveth such a testimony. Of the complaint Wesley says they had among them those whom they ought to have immediately cast out from the flock, holding a doctrine nearly resembling that of Balaam, who taught Balak and the rest of the Moabites to cast a stumbling block before the sons of Israel; they are generally termed the children, but here the sons of Israel, in opposition to the daughters of Moab, by whom Balaam enticed them to fornication and idolatry. To eat things sacrificed to idols, in so idolatrous a city as Pergamos, was in the highest degree hurtful to Christianity, and fornication was constantly joined with the idol-worship of the heathens.

Barnes reports Professor Stuart's suggestion that when the Saviour, as represented in the vision, uttered words, the breath which accompanied them assumed, in the view of John, the form of an igneous two-edged sword; it is more probable, however, Barnes says, that the words which proceeded from his mouth did not assume anything like a form or substance, but that John means to represent them as if they were a sharp sword, since his words cut and penetrate deep, and it was easy to picture him as having a sword proceeding from his mouth. Of the address he says that to know where thou dwellest is to know all the temptations to which they are exposed, all the allurements to sin by which they are surrounded, all the apologies which might be made for what has occurred arising from those circumstances, and all that could be said in commendation of them for having been as faithful as they have been; the sense is that it does much to enable us to judge of character to know where men live, since it is much more easy to be virtuous and pious in some circumstances than in others. Of the complaint he says the charge against this church is somewhat different from that against Ephesus: there the charge was that they had left their first love, but it was spoken in their commendation that they hated the deeds of the Nicolaitanes, whereas here the charge is that they tolerated that sect among them and had among them also those who held the doctrine of Balaam. Their general course had been such that the Saviour could approve it, but he did not approve their tolerating those who held to pernicious practical error, error that tended to sap the very foundation of morals. Ellicott says that, unlike Ephesus and Smyrna, Pergamos was not distinguished as a commercial city, its importance being due to other causes: a striking cone-shaped hill rose from the plain which bordered the northern banks of the Caicus, the hill was considered sacred, and its value as a strong natural fortress was early recognised, so that it was used as a keep and treasury where local chieftains deposited their wealth. Its greatness as a city dated from Eumenes the Second, who was given by the Romans a large surrounding territory and who fixed Pergamos as his royal residence; under his auspices a splendid city rose, rich in public buildings, temples and art galleries, and with a library which rivalled that of Alexandria. Of the throne he says some manuscripts omit the words thy works and read, I know where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is; the word is translated elsewhere throne and should be so here. But why should this pre-eminence in evil be assigned to Pergamos? The answer, Ellicott says, is difficult: some leave it unsolved, saying that in the absence of any historical notice it must remain one of the unsolved riddles of these epistles, while Professor Plumptre suggests that the general character of the city, its worship and customs, in addition to the persecutions which the Christians had encountered, may well account for the description, Aesculapius having been worshipped there. Of the complaint Ellicott says the word few is not to be taken as though the ground of rebuke were a trifling one, since the little leaven might leaven the whole lump, and those who had been brave unto death in the days of persecution had been less temptation-proof against more seductive influences. The church tolerated without remonstrance men holding the teaching of Balaam, and he notes that the word for holding is the same as that used in commendation two verses before, thou holdest fast my name; Israel could not be cursed, but they might be made to bring a curse upon themselves. Robertson says Pergamum lay in a north-easterly direction from Smyrna in the Caicus Valley, some fifty-five miles away, in Mysia, on a lofty hill, a great political and religious centre, which Ramsay calls the royal city, the city of authority. Eumenes the Second extended and embellished it with many great buildings, including a library with two hundred thousand volumes, second only to Alexandria; the Kingdom of Pergamum became a Roman province in the second century before Christ; Pliny termed it the most illustrious city of Asia; and parchment derived its name from Pergamum. It was a rival of Ephesus in its temples to Zeus, Athena and Dionysos. Of the throne he says Satan not simply resided in Pergamum, but had there his throne, the seat of power of a king or judge; the symbol of Asklepios was the serpent, as it is of Satan; there was besides a great throne altar to Zeus cut on the acropolis rock, the symbol, as Swete says, of rampant paganism, and the new Caesar-worship with the recent martyrdom of Antipas made Pergamum indeed a very throne of Satan. Holdest fast my name is a present active indicative meaning dost keep on holding. Of the complaint he says a party in the church that resisted emperor-worship, to the death in the case of Antipas, was yet caught in the insidious wiles of the Nicolaitans which the church in Ephesus withstood; the teaching of Balaam is named because the point of likeness of these heretics with Balaam is here explained, and the imperfect tense gives Balaam's habit, so that he stands, in Charles's phrase, as the prototype of all corrupt teachers, these early Gnostics practising licentiousness as a principle.

debates: Why Satan's throne should be at Pergamos: Ellicott calls the answer difficult and reports that some leave it among the unsolved riddles of these epistles, with Plumptre appealing to the city's worship and customs; Robertson accumulates the serpent of Asklepios, the throne-altar of Zeus on the acropolis and the new Caesar-worship; Wesley says only that the city was above measure given to idolatry

How grave the rebuke is: Ellicott insists the word few does not make it trifling, since the little leaven might leaven the whole lump, and points out that the men are said to hold Balaam's teaching by the very word used to commend the church for holding fast Christ's name

What the sword is: Clarke expounds it as the word of God dissecting the whole mind and slaying the ungodly, where Barnes weighs Stuart's suggestion that the breath of the Saviour's words took visible fiery form and judges it more probable that John means only a comparison

Who Antipas was: Gill reports that some make him pastor of the church while the Apostolical Constitutions give Caius as first bishop, and Wesley dates his martyrdom under Domitian, where Robertson calls it recent and makes it part of what constituted the throne of Satan
outliers: Charles's phrase, quoted by Robertson, that Balaam is the prototype of all corrupt teachers
Clarke's report of the Jewish maxim that Satan must leave any place where a synagogue or academy is established
Gill's list of the other Pergamene martyrs, Carpus, Papulus and the woman Agathonice
Henry's aside that Pergamos may have been a Troy nouveau, as our London was once called
Ramsay's name for Pergamum, quoted by Robertson, the royal city, the city of authority
Robertson's note that parchment takes its name from Pergamum
Stuart's suggestion, reported by Barnes, that the breath of the Saviour's words appeared to John as an igneous two-edged sword
Wesley's note that the text says the sons of Israel, set against the daughters of Moab

15.pericope_label: The hidden manna and the white stone

schools.summary: Gill says these impure heretics sprang up in the time of the apostolic church, but their doctrines were not received and their deeds were hated; here, he thinks, the doctrines of the church of Rome are designed, which in this period took place, forbidding marriage to the priests and recommending celibacy and virginity to others also, which were the source of all uncleanness and abominable lusts, for which pardons and indulgences were given. The call to repent, Gill says, is addressed to those who were truly godly in those times but still retained their communion with these corrupt men and had not yet separated from them, nor protested against these evil doctrines and practices except very coldly, having too much connived at them; therefore they are called upon to repent of their lukewarmness, negligence and sinful compliances.

Clarke refers the doctrine of the Nicolaitans back to his earlier note, and says of the sword that Christ now speaks for their edification and salvation, but that if they do not repent he will shortly declare those judgments which shall unavoidably fall upon them. Of the hidden manna he reports that it was a constant tradition of the Jews that the ark of the covenant, the tables of stone, Aaron's rod, the holy anointing oil and the pot of manna were hidden by King Josiah when Jerusalem was taken by the Chaldeans, and that these shall all be restored in the days of the Messiah; this manna was hidden, but Christ promises to give it to him that is conqueror, since Jesus is the ark, the oil, the rod, the testimony and the manna, and he who is partaker of his grace has all those things in their spiritual meaning and perfection. Of the white stone Clarke offers several suppositions. First, that by it is meant pardon or acquittance and the evidence of it, with an allusion to the custom observed by judges in ancient times, who were accustomed to give their suffrages by white and black pebbles, those who gave the former being for absolving. Secondly, that there is an allusion to conquerors in the public games, who were not only conducted with great pomp into the city to which they belonged but had a white stone given them with their name inscribed on it, which badge entitled them during their whole life to be maintained at the public charge. Thirdly, that the allusion is to the tesserae among the Romans, of which there were several kinds: the tesserae conviviales answered exactly to our cards of invitation or tickets of admission to a public feast or banquet, and when the person invited produced his tessera he was admitted, so that the mention of the hidden manna here may seem to intimate as much; while the tessera of hospitality was a kind of tally, the two parts of which were compared together to ascertain the truth, and Clarke cites the Punic exchange in which one party says that he loves hospitality and loves Carthage where he was born, and the other answers with a blessing. It is very probable, he says, that St John may allude to this. Wesley says that in like manner this angel, as well as the angel at Ephesus, has them that hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans, and suffers them to remain in the flock. If they do not repent, he says, Christ comes to the angel, who will not wholly escape when the others are punished, and will fight with them, not with the Nicolaitans, who are mentioned only by the by, but with the followers of Balaam, and with the sword of his mouth, that is, with his just and fierce displeasure; Balaam himself, Wesley notes, was first withstood by the angel of the Lord with his sword drawn, and afterwards slain with the sword. To him that overcometh, and eateth not of those sacrifices, will he give of the hidden manna, described in the sixth chapter of John, and the new name answers to this, being now hid with Christ in God; the Jewish manna was kept in the ancient ark of the covenant, and the heavenly ark appears under the trumpet of the seventh angel, where also the hidden manna is mentioned again. It seems properly to mean, Wesley says, the full, glorious, everlasting fruition of God. Of the stone he says the ancients on many occasions gave their votes in judgment by small stones, condemning by black and acquitting by white, and sometimes also wrote on small smooth stones, so that here may be an allusion to both; and of the new name, that so Jacob, after his victory, gained the new name of Israel.

Barnes says the meaning may be either that, in addition to those who held the doctrine of Balaam, they had also another class who held the doctrine of the Nicolaitanes, or that the Nicolaitanes held the same doctrine and taught the same thing as Balaam. If but one class is referred to, and the Nicolaitanes held the doctrines of Balaam, then we know what their teaching was; if two classes of false teachers are referred to, then we have no means of knowing what was the peculiarity of the teaching of the Nicolaitanes; and the more natural and obvious construction, Barnes says, is to suppose that the Nicolaitanes taught the same things which Balaam did. Of the threat he says the meaning is that Christ would come against them in judgment, or to punish them: he would come against the church for tolerating them, but his opposition would be principally directed against the Nicolaitanes themselves, since the church would excite his displeasure by retaining them in its bosom, while it was in its power to save them from destruction. If the church would repent, or separate itself from the evil, the Saviour would not come against them; if not, they would feel the vengeance of his sword. The church always suffers, Barnes says, when it has offenders in its bosom. Of the promise he says the hidden manna is the true spiritual food, the food that nourishes the soul, so that the souls of those who overcame would be permitted to partake of that spiritual food which is laid up for the people of God: the Hebrews were supported by manna in the desert, a pot of that manna was laid up in the most holy place to be preserved as a memorial, it is called angels' food and corn of heaven, and it would seem to have been emblematical of that spiritual food by which the people of God are nourished. Ellicott says the connection is that this church, as well as those of old, has such teachers, but that opinions are divided whether we are on this account to identify the Balaamites with the Nicolaitanes and to suppose that both names point to the same sect. The simplest meaning of the passage, he says, seems to be that the temptation to which the Israelites were exposed is used to illustrate the temptations of the Pergamene Church through the teaching of the Nicolaitanes, both temptations leading in the same Antinomian direction; such a tendency was early seen, as passages in Romans, Galatians and Jude show, and is not extinct now, and he quotes Dr Vaughan on the vague and unavowed form it still takes. Of the promise he says it should run: to him that conquereth will I give of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and upon the stone a new name graven, which no man knoweth but he who receiveth it. He notices first that the promise is appropriate, since those who refused to indulge the fleshly appetite are promised gratifications far higher and hidden from the gaze of sense, and secondly that the allusions are not all easy to understand. That to the manna is indeed obvious: Israel ate manna in the wilderness and died, while the Father gives the true bread from heaven that a man may eat thereof and not die, the Son being that Bread of Life, so that he who eateth him shall live by him, and live even though, like Antipas, he die. Robertson says the use of the adverb rendered likewise shows that the Nicolaitans followed Balaam in not obeying the decision of the Conference at Jerusalem about idolatry and fornication, with the result that they encouraged a return to pagan laxity of morals, as Swete puts it; and he adds that some wrongly hold these Nicolaitans to have been Pauline Christians, in the face of what Colossians and Ephesians say. Repent therefore is a first aorist imperative, the tense of urgency, with an inferential particle marking it as a result of their sin; I come is a futuristic present, I am coming, and as with the phrase in the first chapter we do not know how soon quickly is meant to be understood, but it is a real threat. The preposition used here with the verb to war is common in the Greek Old Testament but occurs in the New Testament only in this book, and the verb itself nowhere else except in James; Renan called the clause an eternal roll of thunder from the throne, and Swete says the glorified Christ is in this book a Warrior who fights with the sharp sword of the word. Of the manna Robertson says the golden pot of it was laid up before God in the ark, and that it was believed that Jeremiah hid the ark before the destruction of Jerusalem, where it would not be discovered till Israel was restored, as the second book of Maccabees relates; Christ is the true bread from heaven, and that may be the idea here, so that those faithful to Christ will have transcendent fellowship with him.

debates: Whether the Balaamites and the Nicolaitans are the same party: Barnes states the alternative and judges it more natural that they taught the same thing, Ellicott prefers to treat the wilderness temptation as an illustration rather than an identification, and Robertson makes the adverb rendered likewise decide the point by aligning them with Balaam against the Jerusalem decision

Who hid the manna: Clarke reports the constant Jewish tradition that King Josiah hid the ark, the rod, the oil and the pot of manna at the Chaldean capture of Jerusalem, where Robertson gives the same office to Jeremiah on the authority of Second Maccabees

What the white stone is: Clarke offers the judicial pebble of acquittal, the inscribed stone given to victors in the games entitling them to public maintenance for life, and the Roman tally used both as a ticket of admission to a feast and as a token of hospitality broken between two parties, while Wesley combines the voting stone and the written stone and Ellicott admits the allusions are not all easy

Whom the threat is against: Barnes holds the coming is against the church for tolerating the offenders though aimed principally at the offenders themselves, while Wesley divides the verse between the angel, who will not wholly escape, and the followers of Balaam, with whom alone the fighting is
outliers: Clarke's identification of Christ himself as the ark, the oil, the rod, the testimony and the manna
Clarke's tessera conviviales, answering exactly to our cards of invitation to a feast
Ellicott's remark that the Antinomian tendency was early seen and is not extinct now
Renan's phrase, quoted by Robertson, an eternal roll of thunder from the throne
Swete's description, quoted by Robertson, of the glorified Christ as a Warrior fighting with the sharp sword of the word
Wesley's tracing of the sword back to Numbers, where Balaam was first withstood by the angel with his sword drawn and afterwards slain with the sword
Wesley's comparison of the new name to the Israel that Jacob gained after his victory

18.pericope_label: To Thyatira: much praise, and the woman Jezebel

schools.summary: Gill says a church was formed at Thyatira very likely by the Apostle Paul, Lydia being a native of the place, who with her household was converted and baptized by him at Philippi; though Epiphanius seems to grant, what some heretics objected to the authority of this book, that there was no church at Thyatira when this letter was written. It is certain, however, that there was one in the second century, as the same writer observes, since it was overrun with the Cataphrygian heresy; in the fourth century there was a bishop from Thyatira in the council of Nice, and even in the eighth century the place is still named. Of the works he says they are good works, as appears from the particular enumeration of them afterwards and the commendation of proficiency in them, the last being more than the first. Of the complaint he says the Arabic version renders it, I have a certain complaint against thee, and that the impartiality of Christ may be observed in taking notice of the bad deeds as well as the good ones of his people, with his tenderness in representing them as few; these things he had against them not in a judicial way to their condemnation, but in a providential way, to chastise them for their good. The space to repent he refers to the time of the witnesses, the Waldenses and others, who bore a testimony against the Romish idolatry and denounced the judgment of God in case of impenitence; and as these things were repeated time after time, this may be called a space given to repent in, just as Jezebel had a space given her from the time that Elijah declared the word of the Lord.

Henry says the epistle is directed to the angel of the church of Thyatira, a city of the proconsular Asia, bordering upon Mysia on the north and Lydia on the south, a town of trade, whence came the woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, who, being at Philippi in Macedonia, probably about the business of her calling, heard Paul preach there, and God opened her heart, that she attended to the things that were spoken, and believed, and was baptized, and entertained Paul and Silas there. Whether it was by her means that the gospel was brought to Thyatira, Henry leaves undetermined. The form of each epistle, he notes, is very much the same, so that in this as in the rest we have to consider the inscription, the contents and the conclusion.

Clarke says of the commendation that Christ first sets forth their charity, their love to God and each other and particularly to the poor and distressed, and that hence followed their faith, their fidelity to the grace they had received, and their service or ministration, properly pious and benevolent service to widows, orphans and the poor in general; while their patience is their perseverance under afflictions and persecutions and their continuance in well-doing. He notes that he puts faith before service according to the general consent of the best manuscripts and versions, and takes the works to be the continued labour of love and thorough obedience. Of Jezebel he says there is an allusion to the history of Ahab and Jezebel, and that although we do not know who this Jezebel was, yet from the allusion we may take it for granted she was a woman of power and influence in Thyatira, who corrupted the true religion and harassed the followers of God in that city as Jezebel did in Israel. Instead of that woman Jezebel, Clarke says, many excellent manuscripts and almost all the ancient versions read thy wife Jezebel, which intimates, indeed asserts, that this bad woman was the wife of the bishop of the Church, and his criminality in suffering her was therefore the greater. Of the space given he says this alludes to the history of Jezebel: God first sent Elijah to Ahab to pronounce a severe judgment upon him, upon which Ahab showed tokens of repentance, and so God put off his punishment, and by these means the like punishment pronounced against Jezebel was also put off, so that God gave her time to repent, which she did not, but instead seduced her sons to the same sins. According to the Mosaic law, Clarke adds, the punishment of idolatrous seducers was not to be delayed at all, but God sometimes showed mercy, and much more under the Christian dispensation, though that mercy is often abused. Wesley says the faithful at Thyatira were but a little flock, and bids the reader see how great he is who appeared like a son of man: who hath eyes as a flame of fire, searching the reins and the heart, and feet like fine brass, denoting his immense strength; Job comprises both, his wisdom to discern whatever is amiss and his power to avenge it, in one sentence, that no thought is hidden from him and he can do all things. How different a character this is, Wesley says, from that of the angel of the church at Ephesus: the one could not bear the wicked and hated the works of the Nicolaitans, but had left his first love and first works; the other retained his first love and had more and more works, but did bear the wicked and did not withstand them with becoming vehemence. They are mixed characters both. Love is shown, exercised and improved by serving God and our neighbour, he adds, and so is faith by patience and good works. Of Jezebel he says she ought not to teach at all, and that many of the ancients have delivered that this was the wife of the pastor himself; at Pergamos were many followers of Balaam, at Thyatira one grand deceiver. Jezebel of old led the people of God to open idolatry, and this Jezebel, fitly called by her name from the resemblance between their works, led them to partake in the idolatry of the heathens, seeming to have done it by first enticing them to fornication, just as Balaam did, whereas at Pergamos they were first enticed to idolatry and afterwards to fornication. And I gave her time to repent, Wesley says, shows how great is the power of Christ; but she will not repent, so that though repentance is the gift of God, man may refuse it, and God will not compel.

Barnes says this is the first time in these epistles that the name of the speaker is referred to, since in each other instance there is merely some attribute of the Saviour mentioned; perhaps the severity of the rebuke contemplated here made it proper that there should be a more impressive reference to the authority of the speaker, and hence he is introduced as the Son of God. It is not a reference to him as the Son of man, the common appellation which he gave to himself when on earth, for that might have suggested his humanity only and would not have conveyed the same impression in regard to his authority. Of the commendation he says charity means love, love to God and love to man, and that there is no reason for restricting the word here to the comparatively narrow sense which it now bears; service is ministry, and would seem to include all the service which the church had rendered in the cause of religion, all which was the proper fruit of love; faith is fidelity in the cause of the Redeemer, including not only trust in Christ for salvation but that which is the proper result of such trust. Of Jezebel he says who the individual referred to by that name was is not known, that it is by no means probable this was her real name, but that it seems to have been given to her as expressive of her character and influence; Jezebel was the wife of Ahab, a woman of vast influence over her husband, an influence uniformly exerted for evil, a daughter of Ethbaal king of Tyre and Sidon, an idolater who induced her weak husband to connive at introducing the worship of her own gods. Of the space allowed he says it was probably given after some direct and solemn warning of the evil of her course: the error and sin had been of long standing, but he now resolved to bear with it no longer. It is true of almost every great sinner, Barnes says, that sufficient time is given for repentance and that vengeance is delayed after crime is committed; but it cannot always be deferred, for the period must arrive when no reason shall exist for longer delay. Ellicott says Thyatira was situated between Pergamos and Sardis, a little off the main road which connected these two cities; it was a Macedonian colony founded by Alexander the Great after the overthrow of the Persian empire, and the Macedonian colonists appear to have introduced the worship of Apollo, honoured as the Sun-god, under the name of Tyrimnas. It has been thought by some, he says, that the description here given of Christ, the eyes of flame, was selected in allusion to this worship of the Sun-god under the form of some dazzlingly ornamented image; certainly close commercial intercourse connected the daughter colony with its mother city, and there seem to have been various mercantile guilds in the colony. In the words of commendation, Ellicott says, we find two pairs: the community is commended for charity and service, the outward ministrations which manifest the inner principle of love, and then for faith and patience, the patience being the token of the faith; and the last clause should be read, and thy last works more than the first, so that besides their faith and love they are commended for their progress in good works. Of the complaint he notes that one great manuscript has, I have much against thee, but that the reading, I have against thee that thou lettest alone, is to be preferred; some adopt the reading, thy wife Jezebel, and from these words it has been thought that there was some personal influence at work for evil in Thyatira, though whether in the household of the angel or not is at least doubtful. The sin alleged against her is the same for which the Nicolaitanes are condemned, fornication and the eating of things sacrificed to idols; and if that view be right, the leader of the party is a woman regarded by her followers as a prophetess, as one with a real message from God, but viewed by the Lord of the church otherwise. Of the space he says the reading should be, and I gave her time to repent, and she will not repent of her fornication, or, to repent out of, that is, so as to forsake her fornication; here, as before, we are reminded that true repentance is a repentance whereby we forsake sin. Robertson says Thyatira lay some forty miles south-east of Pergamum, a Lydian city on the edge of Mysia, under Rome since the second century before Christ, a centre of trade especially for the royal purple, the home of Lydia of Philippi, shown by inscriptions to be full of trade guilds, with Apollo the chief deity and no emperor-worship, and a centre of activity by the Nicolaitans with their idolatry and licentiousness under a prophetess who defied the church there; Ramsay calls it Weakness Made Strong. Of the commendation he says four items are given, with a separate feminine article for each, a longer list of graces than that for Ephesus, and that more praise is given in the case of Ephesus and Thyatira when blame follows than in the case of Smyrna and Philadelphia when no fault is found; love comes first in this list in true Johannine fashion, faith here may be faithfulness, and ministry is ministration to the needs of others. Of Jezebel he says the name is symbolical for some prominent woman in the church in Thyatira, like the infamous wife of Ahab who was guilty of whoredom and witchcraft and who sought to drive out the worship of God from Israel; some manuscripts here have the possessive, which Ramsay makes thy woman, but the best copies rightly reject it, since otherwise she is the pastor's wife. Of the space he says the aorist alludes to a definite visit or message of warning to this woman, that the clause and she willeth not is blunt and final, and that the construction is to make a change out of, the usual one with the verb in this book.

debates: Whether the text reads that woman or thy wife: Clarke says many excellent manuscripts and almost all the ancient versions have thy wife, a reading which asserts that she was the bishop's wife and makes his criminality the greater, and Wesley reports the same tradition from the ancients; Ellicott leaves it doubtful whether the influence was in the angel's household; Robertson rejects the possessive because the best copies omit it and because it would make her the pastor's wife

Who Jezebel was: Barnes and Clarke agree the individual cannot be identified and that the name was given for the resemblance of character, where Robertson treats the name as symbolical of a prominent woman in the church and Ellicott of the leader of the party, regarded by her followers as a prophetess with a real message from God

Why the speaker names himself as the Son of God: Barnes holds the severity of the coming rebuke made a more impressive reference to authority proper, since the usual title would have suggested only his humanity, where Ellicott suspects the eyes of flame were chosen in allusion to the city's worship of Apollo as the Sun-god

How the two commended churches compare: Wesley sets Ephesus and Thyatira as mixed characters of opposite kinds, the one hating the wicked but fallen from its first love and the other keeping its love but bearing the wicked, and Robertson observes that more praise is given where blame follows than where no fault is found at all
outliers: Clarke's textual note that he puts faith before service on the consent of the best manuscripts
Ellicott's suggestion that the eyes of flame allude to a dazzlingly ornamented image of the Sun-god
Ellicott's insistence that the Greek is to repent out of, so that true repentance forsakes the sin
Gill's report from Epiphanius that some denied there was any church at Thyatira when the letter was written
Ramsay's name for Thyatira, quoted by Robertson, Weakness Made Strong
Robertson's exclamation against the variant, that otherwise she is the pastor's wife
Wesley's note that at Pergamos idolatry came first and fornication after, and here the order was reversed
Wesley's conclusion that though repentance is the gift of God, man may refuse it and God will not compel

22.pericope_label: The bed of sickness, the depths of Satan, and the morning star

schools.summary: Gill reads the bed as one of sickness and languishing, denoting the sickly, pining and decaying state of the church of Rome, a just retaliation for the bed of luxury and deliciousness she had indulged in; this was threatened and began at the time of the Reformation, and ever since the whore of Rome has been visibly sickening. Her children he takes as her popes, cardinals, priests, Jesuits, monks and friars and all who join in the Romish apostasy, who shall be killed with death, that is, either utterly extirpated in God's own time or killed with the second death, since the word used alone signifies the plague. Of the address to the rest he notes that the copulative is left out in the Alexandrian copy and the Complutensian edition, and that the persons spoken to are the pastor with his colleagues and all the rest of the faithful, which shows that this epistle, and so the rest, were not written to the pastors only but to the churches. That which they already have is the faithful word, the form of sound words, the mystery and doctrine of faith received from Christ and his apostles, which they held and are here exhorted to hold fast. He that overcometh, Gill says, is he that overcomes Jezebel and her idolatries and all that commit adultery with her, who is not drawn into the same evil practices but stands his ground against the Romish antichrist. The rod of iron he takes either of the Gospel, which is the rod of Christ's strength, or of the great strictness and severity with which the man of sin will be used by the saints of the most High when they take away his dominion. The morning star he refers to an illustrious appearance of Christ at the close of this church state, and to the reformation by Luther and Calvin, which is the phosphorus or morning star to the spiritual reign of Christ, the present twilight lying between the appearance of the morning star and the glorious day.

Clarke says the bed alludes to the same history: Ahaziah, son of Ahab and Jezebel, by his mother's ill instruction and example followed her ways, and God punished him by making him fall, as is supposed, from the top of the terrace over his house, and so to be bedridden for a long time under great anguish, designing thereby to give him time to repent; but when instead of that he sent to consult Baalzebub, Elijah was sent to pronounce a final doom. Of the children he says the meaning is, I will certainly destroy her offspring and memory and thereby ruin her designs: Jezebel's two sons, being both kings, were both slain, and after that all the seventy sons of Ahab, in all which the hand of God was very visible, and in the same manner God predicts the destruction of the heretics and heresies referred to. Of the address to the rest he prefers the Complutensian reading, which evidently shows that the rest of the epistle wholly concerns the faithful who have not received the former doctrine of error; and the promise to put upon them no other burden is a commendation of the sound part of the Church, that they have no need of any new exhortation or charge, no new advice but to persevere as usual. That which ye have is the pure doctrine of the Gospel, to be held fast till Christ comes to execute the judgments he has threatened. Of the power over the nations Clarke says every witness of Christ has power to confute and confound all the false doctrines and maxims of the nations of the world, for Christianity shall at last rule over all. The rod of iron means that he shall restrain vice by the strictest administration of justice, and those who finally despise the word and rebel shall be broken and destroyed so as never more to be able to make head against the truth; this seems to refer to the heathen world, and perhaps Constantine the Great may be intended, who, when he overcame Licinius, became the instrument in God's hand of destroying idolatry over the whole Roman empire, which was so effectually broken as to be ever after like the fragments of an earthen vessel. The morning star means he shall have the brightest and most glorious empire next to that of Christ himself; and it is certain, Clarke says, that the Roman empire under Constantine the Great was the brightest emblem of the latter day glory which has ever yet been exhibited to the world, since sun, moon and stars are emblems in prophetic language of empires, kingdoms and states, and as the morning star immediately precedes the rising of the sun, it probably here intends an empire which should usher in the universal day. Of the closing summons he says, let every Christian pay the strictest regard to these predictions of Christ, and let them have a suitable influence on his heart and life. Wesley says the casting into a bed means into great affliction, and that those who commit either carnal or spiritual adultery with her are included unless they repent, she having had her time before; it is observable, he adds, that the angel of the church at Thyatira was only blamed for suffering her, and that this fault ceased when God took vengeance on her, so that he is not expressly exhorted to repent, though it is implied. The killing of her children is death by the plague or by some manifest stroke of God's hand, and probably the remarkable vengeance taken on her children was the token of the certainty of all the rest; the reins are the desires and the hearts the thoughts. Of those who have not known the depths of Satan Wesley exclaims, O happy ignorance: they were continually boasting of the deep things which they taught, and our Lord owns they were deep, even deep as hell, for they were the very depths of Satan; and he asks whether these were the same of which Martin Luther speaks, adding that it is well if there are not some of his countrymen now in England who know them too well. Of the promise he says the meaning is, I will give him to share with me in that glorious victory which the Father hath promised me over all the nations who as yet resist me; the rod of iron is irresistible power, employed on those only who will not otherwise submit, and who will hereby be totally conquered. Thou, O Jesus, art the morning star, Wesley says: O give thyself to me, then will I desire no sun, only thee, who art the sun also; he whom this star enlightens has always morning and no evening. The duties and promises here answer each other, since the valiant conqueror has power over the stubborn nations, and he that, after having conquered his enemies, keeps the works of Christ to the end, shall have the morning star, an unspeakable brightness and peaceable dominion in him.

Barnes says the bed is not a bed of ease but a bed of pain, there being evidently a purpose to contrast this with her former condition: the harlot's bed and a sick bed are thus brought together, as they often are in fact in the dispensations of Providence and the righteous judgment of God, since one cannot be indulged without leading on, sooner or later, to the horrid sufferings of the other. Of the children he says it has been made a question whether the word is to be taken literally or figuratively, that the word itself would admit of either interpretation, and that there is nothing in the connection by which its meaning here can be determined; if literally, it is in accordance with what is often threatened in the Scriptures. Of the address to the rest he notes that the connective is omitted in many manuscripts and versions and in the critical editions of Griesbach, Tittmann and Hahn, and that the connection demands its omission, since as the received text stands it would seem that what is said was addressed to those who had received that doctrine as well as to others, whereas the declaration pertains manifestly to those who had not received it. That which ye have means all that there is of truth and purity remaining among you, to be retained faithfully till he comes to receive them to himself. Of the promise he says the evident meaning is that, in accordance with the uniform promise made to the redeemed in the New Testament, they would partake of the final triumph and glory of the Saviour and be associated with him; it is not said that they would have exclusive power over the nations or that they would hold offices. In the rod of iron there is an allusion to the second Psalm, with a slight change, he shall rule instead of thou shalt break, in order to adapt the language to the purpose of the speaker, the allusion in the Psalm being to the Messiah as reigning triumphant over the nations. The morning star, Barnes says, is that bright planet Venus which at some seasons of the year appears so beautifully in the east, leading on the morning, the harbinger of the day; it is one of the most beautiful objects in nature and susceptible of a great variety of uses for illustration, appearing as the darkness passes away, an indication that the morning comes, intermingled with the first rays of the light of the sun and seeming to be a herald to announce the coming of that glorious luminary. Ellicott says the chamber of voluptuousness will become the chamber of sickness, and the spot of the sin shall be the scene of the punishment. Her children is to be understood of her followers: the so-called prophetess led the way in looseness of morals under the pretence of some deeper knowledge, she had her associates and their disciples, the evil and the evil consequences would grow, the disciples outrun their teachers, and more than tribulation, namely death, is their penalty. On the address to the rest he would omit the connective, and of the depths he says these teachers, as was the case with the Gnostics, professed to have a deeper insight into mysteries, the deep things of God; they may have garnished their speech with this very phrase, borrowed in sound though not in sense from First Corinthians, and may even have boasted of their knowledge of Satan, but such knowledge was purchased too dearly, and better off were they who were simple concerning evil. The morning star he calls the pledge of the coming day, both for the waiting witnesses and for the ungodly who loved darkness because their deeds were evil, the earnest of the sovereignty of light over darkness, when the children of the day would be manifest and shine as the stars for ever and ever. Robertson says the present tense is used rather than the future since judgment is imminent, and quotes Beckwith, a bed of sickness in contrast with the bed of adultery; those who commit adultery with her are the actual paramours of the woman Jezebel, guilty of both fornication and adultery. I will kill with death is a future with the cognate phrase in the sense of pestilence, as in Ezekiel; her children are either her actual children, like the fate of Ahab's sons, or, as Swete has it, her spiritual progeny who have completely accepted her Nicolaitan practices. To you the rest means those who hold out against Jezebel, not necessarily a minority; the relative is generic of the class; and know not is a second aorist meaning did not come to know by experience. Hold fast is a first aorist imperative, either ingressive, get a grip on, or constative, hold on as a single decisive effort, in contrast with the present imperative used later for keeping on holding. He that overcometh and he that keepeth are present active articular participles in the nominative absolute, resumed by the dative. Authority over the nations comes from the second Psalm, the followers of the Messiah sharing in his victory over his enemies; he shall rule is a future of the verb meaning to shepherd, continuing the quotation, the rod being the royal sceptre and indicating rigorous rule, and the vessels of the potter using an old adjective found only here in the New Testament. As I also have received is a perfect active indicative, Christ still possessing the power from the Father; and of the morning star Robertson notes that in the last chapter Christ is the bright morning star, so that the victor will have Christ himself.

debates: What the morning star means: Clarke takes it politically, of the brightest and most glorious empire next to Christ's own, naming the Roman empire under Constantine as the brightest emblem of the latter day glory yet exhibited, while Robertson refuses the transfer and holds that since Christ is himself the bright morning star of the last chapter, the victor will have Christ himself; Wesley turns it into a prayer for Christ's own presence

Whether her children are literal or figurative: Barnes says the word admits of either and nothing in the connection decides it, Robertson offers both with Swete's spiritual progeny as the alternative, Clarke keeps to the history of Ahab's sons, and Ellicott takes them without hesitation for her followers

Whether the connective should stand before the rest: Barnes reports its omission in many manuscripts and in the editions of Griesbach, Tittmann and Hahn and says the connection demands it be dropped, and Clarke prefers the Complutensian reading for the same reason, since it shows that the remainder of the epistle concerns the faithful only

What the rod of iron does: Clarke reads it of the strictest administration of justice against the heathen world and suggests Constantine as the instrument, where Wesley makes it irresistible power employed only on those who will not otherwise submit, and Gill takes it either of the Gospel or of the severity with which the man of sin will be used
outliers: Beckwith's phrase, quoted by Robertson, a bed of sickness in contrast with the bed of adultery
Clarke's account of Ahaziah bedridden after his fall, given time to repent and sending instead to consult Baalzebub
Ellicott's epigram that the spot of the sin shall be the scene of the punishment
Ellicott's suggestion that the false teachers used the phrase depths of Satan themselves, borrowed in sound though not in sense from First Corinthians
Gill's note that the address to the rest shows these epistles were written not to the pastors only but to the churches
Wesley's aside asking whether these were the depths of which Luther speaks, and whether some of his countrymen in England know them too well
Wesley's prayer, that he whom this star enlightens has always morning and no evening
